That may mean coaching a manager, building an internal tool, making business data useful, or automating a repetitive task. The solution should fit the problem.

The hidden work behind polished results: patience, practice, and the small decisions that make good work possible.
The hidden work behind good work — Vitalijs Arkulinskis
The polished result is visible. The patience, practice, and problem-solving that made it possible usually aren’t.
We notice the smooth presentation, the thoughtful design, the calm response in a difficult moment. What we don’t see is everything that happened before it looked effortless.

Good work has a backstage. It is the repetition that builds confidence, the awkward first attempts, the questions asked twice, the small problems caught before they become large ones. We often call the finished result talent or instinct, as if it arrived fully formed.

Teams can fall into the same trap. We reward visible outcomes and overlook the effort that makes those outcomes repeatable: sharing context, helping a colleague, keeping a process healthy, learning from a mistake. When that work stays invisible, people can feel that only the final flourish counts.

Recognizing the work behind the work changes what we value. It lets us learn from the process, improve it, and give credit where it belongs. Mastery is rarely one grand gesture. More often, it is many small acts of attention sustained over time.
The next time something feels effortless, look a little closer. There may be a lot of care underneath.
New technologies are an invitation to experiment. Start with the problem, and learn from trying a new tool.
Looking for problems for AI to solve — Vitalijs Arkulinskis
A new tool can be exciting before we know what to do with it. That’s a reason to experiment—and a reason to stay curious about the problem.

Every powerful new technology creates a period of exuberance. People try it everywhere, including in places where the old method is already working. It can look like a solution searching for a problem.

But experimentation is part of how we learn what a technology is actually good for. Early uses are often clumsy. They reveal what is possible, where the limits are, and which assumptions deserve a second look.
Keep the problem in the room

The useful question isn’t simply whether AI can be added to a task. It is whether the task matters, what a better outcome looks like, and whether the tool can help us reach it safely and reliably. Sometimes the experiment shows that a simpler approach is still best. Sometimes it opens a route that wasn’t practical before.

That distinction matters in business. A clever demo is not the same as a dependable process. Consider the people who will rely on the result, the quality of the information going in, and what happens when the system gets it wrong. Use experiments to learn, then judge the outcome against the real work.
Curiosity moves technology forward. Clear problems help curiosity turn into value.
Why unconventional product ideas deserve curiosity: customers value delight and meaning as well as function.
Don’t dismiss the silly idea — Vitalijs Arkulinskis
What looks unnecessary to one person might bring joy, identity, or just the right kind of surprise to someone else.

Some successful products look absurd when you describe them plainly. A blanket with sleeves. A rock sold as a pet. A tiny video that makes you laugh on a busy day. It is tempting to judge an idea by whether it seems useful to us.

But usefulness isn’t only speed or convenience. People choose things for delight, belonging, expression, comfort, and many other reasons. A product can meet a need that its creator didn’t expect—or that a spreadsheet doesn’t capture.

That doesn’t mean every unconventional idea is secretly brilliant. It means a quick dismissal can close off learning. Ask who might love it, what moment it fits into, and what feeling or job it serves. Then put a small version in front of real people and listen.

Customers may not describe the solution before it exists. They can still show us what they value when they encounter it. The product team’s job is to notice the signal, including when it comes from a surprising place.
So keep a little room for the playful, the strange, and the not-quite-practical. Sometimes the odd idea is only odd until you understand who it is for.
How arkvital.com handles your information: no cookies, no tracking, no forms. Who to contact about your privacy.
This site doesn’t use cookies, analytics, ads or forms. Here is what little happens to your information when you visit, and who to ask about it.

arkvital.com is the website of Vitalijs Arkulinskis, doing business as Arkvital, in Montréal, Québec, Canada. I’m responsible for the personal information described here and I’m the person in charge of protecting it. You can reach me at
. The apps I run each have their own Privacy & Terms page.
There are no forms, no accounts and no comments here. The site itself sets no cookies and stores nothing in your browser. It has no analytics, tracking pixels or advertising.

The pages are served by Firebase Hosting (Google LLC, United States). Like any web host, it briefly records technical details of each visit, such as your IP address, browser type and the pages requested, to deliver the site and keep it secure.
The fonts come from Google Fonts (Google LLC, United States). When a page loads, your browser sends your IP address and browser details to Google.

The Interests page shows two YouTube videos. They stay as plain pictures until you press play. Only then does your browser load the player from YouTube (Google LLC, United States, in its privacy-enhanced mode), which receives your IP address and browser details and may store information in your browser under Google’s own privacy policy.

Google acts under its own privacy commitments and relies on the EU–US Data Privacy Framework and standard contractual clauses for information that leaves Canada or Europe. Before using these services, I assessed that they protect information adequately.
When you contact me or book a call

If you write to me, I use your name, email address and message only to reply and to work with you. I keep them as long as our conversation or work together needs them, plus any period the law requires for business records.

The “Talk with me” buttons open TidyCal (tidycal.com), a separate booking service with its own privacy policy. When you book, TidyCal collects the details you enter (such as your name, email address and what you’d like to discuss) and sends them to me so we can meet. I use them only for that meeting and our follow-up.
and the other websites linked from here are run by others, under their own privacy policies.
I never sell your information, use it for advertising, add you to a mailing list without asking, or use it to train AI models.
